headline: Ten Songs Out of the Long Weather
standfirst: It took Radiohead more than two years, a failed producer, a near break-up and a summer on the road to make their warmest record. Then they gave it away for whatever you wanted to pay, and the music still turned out to be the bigger story.

sections.heading: Free, and stuck
paragraphs: By the end of 2004 Radiohead had nothing they were obliged to do. The world tour for *Hail to the Thief* was over, and that record had been the last one owed under their contract with EMI. For the first time since they were students, nobody was waiting on a Radiohead album. Philip Selway later described the pause as a natural place to stop and take stock; the *New York Times* took to calling them the most popular unsigned band in the world.

Freedom, it turned out, was hard to work in. When the five of them gathered at their Oxfordshire studio in March 2005 they did so without Nigel Godrich, the producer who had been in the room for every album since *OK Computer*. Accounts differ on why. Ed O'Brien suggested they had grown too comfortable with one another; Colin Greenwood said Godrich was simply busy with Beck and Charlotte Gainsbourg. Either way, the band were on their own, and every one of them had become a father.

Sessions proper began that August. They posted occasional updates on a new band blog, Dead Air Space, but the news underneath was not good. Thom Yorke would later describe long stretches in the studio going nowhere at all. There was no deadline, no label and no producer pushing them toward an ending, and the songs refused to settle.

pullQuote.text: Freedom, it turned out, was hard to work in.

sections.heading: Songs with long shadows
paragraphs: What makes *In Rainbows* unusual is that many of its songs were already old by the time anyone heard them on record. The most extreme case is [[Nude]]. Radiohead first recorded it with Godrich during the earliest sessions for *OK Computer*, a version built around Hammond organ and a debt to Al Green. They were pleased with it at first, then went off it. Yorke played it solo in Japan in the late 1990s, the band returned to it during both *Kid A* and *Hail to the Thief*, and in 2004 Yorke admitted he had toyed with handing it to Elvis Costello and the Attractions, who he felt might do it better. For a decade it was one of the best-known Radiohead songs that did not officially exist.

Other songs surfaced in public long before they were finished. In July 2005, at the Ether festival in London, Yorke and Jonny Greenwood performed an early [[Weird Fishes / Arpeggi]] with the London Sinfonietta and the Arab Orchestra of Nazareth. That year Yorke also sang [[House of Cards]] alone on an acoustic guitar at a Trade Justice rally in London, and on the web series *From the Basement* he played [[Videotape]] alongside two songs that would end up on the album's companion disc.

Meanwhile Yorke was building something new on his laptop: a stuttering, clapping rhythm in five beats to the bar, prompted by the handclap groove of a Peaches song. It would become [[15 Step]], the record's opening track. Radiohead teased it on their blog in March 2006, months before anyone could hear it.

sections.heading: The dark winter, and the road out
paragraphs: In December 2005 the band brought in Spike Stent, a producer and mixer whose credits ran from U2 to Björk, to help them make sense of what they had. Stent listened to their self-produced recordings and agreed that they were not good enough. The partnership that followed did not work either, and its recordings would eventually be thrown away.

Things got bad enough that their management raised the possibility of the band breaking up. Brian Message, a partner in the firm, later framed it as simple honesty: if something isn't working, you have to say so. O'Brien said what kept them going was the conviction that, underneath the mess, the songs themselves were strong. He also admitted thinking this might be the last Radiohead album, and wanting it to be one worthy of the band's legacy.

Their solution was to leave the studio. In May and June 2006 Radiohead toured Europe and North America for the first time since 2004, then came back for European festivals in August, and they filled the sets with unreleased songs. Playing them to crowds forced the band to finish writing them. Yorke told the *New York Times* that, far from being an ordeal, the tour had been enormous fun; in his words, “It felt like being 16 again.”

Some songs were born on that tour almost in real time. Yorke and Jonny Greenwood first played [[Bodysnatchers]] as a duo in May 2006 at a climate-change benefit at Koko in London. [[15 Step]] opened the band's first show of the tour in Copenhagen and stayed in the set from then on. A rough early version of [[Jigsaw Falling Into Place]] went out under the working title “Open Pick”. And on 20 June, at the Auditorium Theatre in Chicago, Yorke introduced [[All I Need]] by warning the audience that they had only sketched it out earlier that day. A fan filmed it on a phone and put it on YouTube, and the band later used that crackly clip as a reference in the studio. Yorke said the rawness of it was exactly what excited him.

pullQuote.text: Playing them to crowds forced the band to finish writing them.

sections.heading: A house with holes in the floor
paragraphs: After the tour, Radiohead scrapped the Stent recordings and asked Nigel Godrich back. His first job was to make them stop tinkering. He bounced their rhythm tracks down to a single track so that they could no longer be pulled apart and re-edited, which meant every decision had to be lived with. Colin Greenwood put the logic plainly: “The idea was to make us commit to something.” He compared it to sampling themselves, sounds mashed together until they began to interact.

Godrich also chose where they would work. For three weeks in October 2006 the band set up in Tottenham House, a crumbling Georgian country house in Wiltshire, roughly 45 miles from Oxford. It was in such poor repair that they slept in caravans parked beside it. Yorke later recalled missing window panes, rain coming in and whole areas of the building nobody went into, and he believed the strange atmosphere seeped into the music. They played on guitars borrowed from Johnny Marr, among them a 1957 Gibson Les Paul Gold Top, and Colin picked up temporary hearing damage from a faulty pair of headphones.

The sessions finally moved. Yorke wrote on Dead Air Space that the record had properly begun. [[Bodysnatchers]] was cut there, and it remains the only track on the album recorded as a live take with all five playing together, a lurching, overdriven thing Yorke described as a cross between Neu! and dodgy hippy rock, fuelled by what he called a period of hyperactive mania. Its ideas came from Victorian ghost stories, *The Stepford Wives* and a sense of being trapped inside one's own body. [[Jigsaw Falling Into Place]] was recorded at Tottenham House too, its rushing bass line carrying a story Yorke drew from nights out drinking in Oxford: the thrill of a crowded night and the darker blur that follows it.

Another song took shape in the same restless spirit. [[Reckoner]] began as a coda to a much heavier song of the same name that Radiohead had played live back in 2001. The coda grew into a song of its own and kept the title; Yorke and Jonny Greenwood later reworked the original, and it appeared in 2009 as Yorke's single “FeelingPulledApartByHorses”. Godrich remembered people all over the house shaking things and building a groove, which was then chopped into pieces and reassembled. Over the top went Yorke's falsetto, a looping guitar figure he called a clumsy tribute to John Frusciante, piano, and strings arranged by Jonny Greenwood. Yorke called it a love song, more or less, and said one of its lines was the centre of the whole album, the point everything moved toward and then away from.

pullQuote.text: Every decision had to be lived with.

sections.heading: Building the rooms inside the songs
paragraphs: In December 2006 work moved to Halswell House near Taunton in Somerset and to Godrich's studio at the Hospital Club in Covent Garden. [[Nude]] was completed in London. Its rebirth had begun with a new bass line from Colin Greenwood, which Godrich said gave the old, straight song a rhythmic flow it had always lacked; the band also cut a chorus and wrote a new ending. They recorded three takes, kept the last, and added overdubs at the Hospital Club. Godrich later argued that every song has a moment when it is most alive, that [[Nude]] had missed its moment the first time, and that a new arrangement let the band find it again. Yorke, who had once thought the song sat too high and felt too delicate for him, came to love it for exactly those reasons.

[[Videotape]] was the hardest of all. Yorke described its making as “absolute agony”, a song pushed through every possible arrangement. He had first imagined it as a post-rave trance track in the manner of the techno producer Surgeon; on the 2006 tour it was a band performance that climbed to a big finish on Selway's drums. Godrich and Jonny Greenwood stripped it back to piano, voice and the ticking of a Roland TR-909 drum machine, and Greenwood became fixated on shifting where the bar seems to begin, so that the listener's sense of the downbeat quietly slips. A song shadowed by mortality became the album's spare, devastating close.

Godrich's habit of mixing versions served [[All I Need]], which was assembled from four different recordings. Jonny Greenwood wanted to capture the wall of white noise a loud band makes in a room, a sound that never quite happens in a studio, so he had the strings of the Millennia Ensemble play every note of the scale, smothering the frequencies, and added his own viola. O'Brien strung a guitar with four low E strings for extra weight. The result is a slow-burning love song about longing that breaks open when Selway's cymbals finally crash in.

Elsewhere the textures are lighter. [[Weird Fishes / Arpeggi]] uses interlocking, gradually shifting arpeggios influenced by Steve Reich's phase music; O'Brien pointed to it as the song that was allowed to be truly epic. [[Faust Arp]] is a brief interlude of fingerpicked acoustic guitar and sweeping strings, its title a nod to the German krautrock band Faust. And [[House of Cards]], once tried with an R.E.M.-style bass riff and, at Jonny Greenwood's urging, briefly imagined as an Iggy Pop song, was reworked by Yorke and Selway into the hazy, unhurried groove Yorke called mellow and summery, likening it to Fleetwood Mac's “Albatross”.

Even the cheers at the end of [[15 Step]] have a story. Godrich and Colin Greenwood recorded a group of children at the Matrix Arts Centre in Oxfordshire, and their voices sit, bright and oblivious, against a lyric shadowed by deception and dread.

pullQuote.text: A song shadowed by mortality became the album's spare, devastating close.

sections.heading: Forty-five minutes, and a toxic rainbow
paragraphs: Work resumed in Oxfordshire in January 2007, and by June recording was done, and Godrich posted clips from the studio online. The band had felt *Hail to the Thief* ran too long, and this time they wanted a short, complete statement. Yorke spoke of believing in the rock album as an art form and of aiming for about 45 minutes. They chose ten songs and set the rest aside for a second disc. Bob Ludwig mastered the record at Gateway Mastering in New York in July 2007. Yorke said this was an album about transience and mortality rather than politics, one that begins in one place and ends somewhere entirely different, and the sequence bears him out: it opens in skittering unease and closes alone at a piano.

Stanley Donwood, the band's longtime artist, worked alongside the band throughout, putting images up in the studio and on the studio computer for them to react to, and posting new pictures daily on the band's website, none of which made the final package. He had set out to make work about suburban life, but as the music grew more organic, sensual and sexual he switched to wax and syringes, photographic etching, prints dropped into acid baths and wax flung at paper, with NASA's space photography as a reference point. What emerged was colour that looks spilled rather than painted. Donwood described it to *NME* in a phrase that suits the record well: “It's a rainbow but it is very toxic,” more like the sheen of oil on a puddle than anything in the sky. The title itself was picked partly because it was open and unprovocative, and because it matched his pictures. The cover was kept back until the CD came out.

sections.heading: It's up to you
paragraphs: In the weeks before the announcement, Radiohead's website filled with coded messages; fans who cracked them found fragments of [[Bodysnatchers]]. Then, on 1 October, Jonny Greenwood posted a short note on the blog: the new album was finished, it was called *In Rainbows*, and it would be out in ten days. The link beneath it let anyone pre-order a download. Anyone could type in their own price, including nothing at all. The idea had come from the band's managers, Bryce Edge and Chris Hufford, who had been kicking around ideas while the record dragged on.

The download went live at about 5:30am GMT on 10 October 2007, a ZIP file of the ten tracks as 160 kbps MP3s with no copy protection. For fans who wanted something to hold there was a discbox, sold for £40 from the band's site: the album on CD and on two heavyweight 12-inch records at 45rpm, a second CD of eight more songs, and artwork, all bound in a hardback book and slipcase, shipping that December. The regular CD followed on 31 December on the independent label XL, with TBD Records issuing it in the US on 1 January 2008. It came in a plain case with stickers so that owners could make their own cover.

The release became a news story far beyond music. *Time* called it the most important release in the recent history of the music business; others, from Trent Reznor to Lily Allen, attacked it, either for not going far enough or for undercutting less famous musicians. In the background, EMI had just been bought by the private equity firm Terra Firma, talks over a new deal had collapsed, and EMI soon issued a box set of the band's older albums in the same week as the discbox. Radiohead's management insisted the scheme was a solution for Radiohead, not for the industry, and the band never repeated it.

pullQuote.text: Anyone could type in their own price, including nothing at all.

sections.heading: The warm one
paragraphs: The noise around the price could have buried the songs. It did the opposite. When the CD reached shops it went to number one in both the UK and the US, and by October 2008 the album had sold three million copies worldwide; it was also the best-selling vinyl album of 2008. [[Nude]] became the band's first American top-40 single since “Creep”. [[House of Cards]] got a video made without cameras, built from laser-scanned data, and the band released the separate parts of [[Reckoner]] for fans to remix. At the Grammys in February 2009, *In Rainbows* won Best Alternative Music Album and Best Boxed or Special Limited Edition Package, was nominated for Album of the Year, and Yorke and Jonny Greenwood played [[15 Step]] with the USC Marching Band.

Critics heard the album the band had hoped to make. Reviewers kept coming back to the same words: human, warm, romantic, sensual, a group reconnecting with melody without letting go of their strangeness. Billboard and Mojo named it the best album of 2007, the Mercury Prize put it on its shortlist, and it turned up on many lists of the decade's best records, including those of *Rolling Stone*, *NME* and the *Guardian*. Years later, Selway and O'Brien both named it their favourite Radiohead album, Selway describing it as twenty years of learning finally landing in a concise way.

It is easy to hear why. After all the false starts, *In Rainbows* sounds like five people in a room who have stopped trying to outrun what they are. The rhythms are intricate but never cold; the strings swell rather than loom; the love songs, from [[All I Need]] to [[Reckoner]], are unguarded in a way Radiohead had rarely allowed. Its long, fraught gestation left no trace of struggle on the surface. What remains is the feeling of something arriving whole, ten songs moving from the jittery opening of [[15 Step]] to the hush of [[Videotape]], with the gentle drift of [[Faust Arp]] and the slow unfurling of [[Weird Fishes / Arpeggi]] along the way. More than a decade on, it is still the Radiohead record people reach for when they want to be held rather than unsettled.

pullQuote.text: Its long, fraught gestation left no trace of struggle on the surface.
